articles.title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
articles.summary: There were hundreds of arrests as protesters took to the streets in cities across France for the third weekend in a row.
body: Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.

An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.

Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
Police officers hit with Molotov cocktails during Paris protest
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.

The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."

Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.

French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".

France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.

Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

articles.title: Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
articles.summary: The author of Jasper Jones and Runt pleaded guilty in May after police raided his home months earlier.
body: The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".

In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.

She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.

"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.

Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

articles.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
articles.summary: Five officers from the Hamas-run police have been killed in Khan Younis and three people, including a child, killed in Gaza City, officials say.
body: Mourners attend the funeral of five Palestinians, who were killed in an Israeli strike
Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.

In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel.

"My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"

At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.

Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.
The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

articles.title: Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
articles.summary: The new police unit is a security measure in response to last year's deadly shooting attack at a Hanukkah festival.
body: Armed police officers on patrol outside Sydney's Luna Park
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles – an unfamiliar sight for most residents.

New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl – were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.

But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.

"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

articles.title: University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash
articles.summary: Marta Shahbazi was an "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist", says the laboratory where she worked.
body: Dr Marta Shahbazi, pictured in 2024, was travelling to collect a prize at an awards ceremony in her native Spain when she died
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.

The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.

She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.

The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.

"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi joined the Cambridge laboratory in 2020
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.

"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

articles.title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
articles.summary: Police in Frankfurt say "violent riots" took place in the city centre, with unrest also reported in Berlin, Hamburg and Cologne.
body: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday and clashes erupted with police there and in other German cities after largely peaceful mass protests over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who targeted emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands earlier joined the demonstrations organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police, AFP news agency reported. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.

Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
While protests during the day were largely peaceful, the demonstrations turned violent as night fell.

In a post on X, Frankfurt police said that "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre. The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
In later updates, officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect.

Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.

Poseck said: "We all have those images from France in our minds – looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."

articles.title: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
articles.summary: It comes amid growing protests over a voter roll revision exercise feared to leave 130 million voters off rolls.
body: Rahul Gandhi has called on people to gather at the protest site in large numbers
Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.
The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.
Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.
The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.

But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.

The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.
Protests have been going on for weeks seeking CEC Kumar's resignation and electoral reforms
The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
But concerns over the revision process have continued, with the opposition parties, the CJP and student groups organising a number of protests in Delhi and other Indian cities.
On Saturday, opposition leaders staged a symbolic impeachment of Kumar at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence in Delhi.

The mock parliamentary session, presided over by former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar, saw leaders accuse the election chief of "conspiring to steal elections" and deliberately removing 130 million voters from electoral rolls.

Kharge, who is also the leader of the opposition in parliament's upper house, moved a symbolic motion seeking Kumar's removal, accusing him of undermining the electoral process and committing an act of "treason against the nation and the Constitution of India".
Several people whose names had been removed from electoral rolls during the revision exercise also attended the event.
The proceedings were purely symbolic and had no legal standing. Under Indian law, the chief election commissioner can only be removed through a formal parliamentary process.
Opposition alliance held a mock impeachment of CEC Kumar on Saturday

Last month, Congress MP and leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation.
"The march was just the trailer," a party leader told the BBC, adding that "Sunday's rally will be several times bigger than that".

Ahead of the rally, Gandhi said their protest was against "the demolition of Indian democracy", adding that "all the opposition parties and everybody who wants to come, political or non-political, is welcome".
"There is huge anger, huge emotional pain because millions are being disenfranchised," he said.
"We are all standing together because we are defending the Constitution. We are defending the idea of India. We are defending the vote, which is the expression of all Indians."
Thousands gathered for the last Congress rally in Delhi on 12 October

Delhi police have given permission to hold Sunday's rally, but it comes with several conditions. Media reports say the rally must end by 5pm, CCTV cameras must be installed at the venue and no marches will be allowed outside the designated protest site.
The planned mega rally has also divided opinion among traders in Chandni Chowk, one of Delhi's oldest and busiest markets, located less than a kilometre from Ramlila Maidan.
Earlier this week, a group of traders said the protest could hurt business during the festive season, coming just a week before Diwali.
But a rival group of traders said they supported Gandhi's rally and criticised the BJP for taking out a march through the market on Thursday, saying that disrupted the festive season more.
Authorities have deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel across the city, including the roads leading up to Ramlila Grounds, Sunday's protest venue.
The opposition, which has been preparing for the rally for days now, has accused the government of trying to stop people from travelling to Delhi to take part in the protest.
Leaders of the ruling BJP party also carried out a march in Chandni Chowk market on Thursday

Rahul Gandhi has appealed to people to turn up in large numbers. "Don't worry about the police, don't worry about lathis [batons] - the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics," he wrote on X.
His comments come amid growing concerns about the policing of recent protests in the capital.
On 10 October, thousands of security personnel were deployed and large parts of the city were shut down to thwart protests called by the CJP against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

All of the top CJP leaders were detained and many demonstrators were beaten and dragged through the streets to break up their protests. BBC reporters covering demonstrations saw, external police dragging away protesters and using batons on some of them.
The CJP has publicly backed the INDIA bloc rally, but it is unclear whether its senior leaders will attend.

articles.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
articles.summary: Two analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprit.
body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
It said it had replenished the assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean

The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.

The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group called The Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, as the likely culprits.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange last year.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

articles.title: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology
articles.summary: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
body: Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.

The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event to launch a “structured dialogue” into what form an apology might take.
UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate.
In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.

Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs.

“In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past.”

Burnham set out his intention to look at a possible apology in an article for the Guardian on Saturday, in which he said the UK should “show leadership again today” as it had done in efforts to end the transatlantic slave trade.

Asked why Burnham believed an apology was needed, his official spokesperson said: “The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration.” Having conversations about an apology would do this, and was also the right thing to do, he said.
Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” about the slave trade and Britain’s role in it in 2006, but stopped short of a formal apology.

Burnham intended to go further, his spokesperson said. “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today.
Related: Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?

“That is distinct from a formal apology. We are opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.

“We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they have asked for.”
Burnham is scheduled to take part in a series of assemblies at Chogm, as well as bilateral meetings with other leaders.

There was no single event set aside to discuss slavery or an apology, but discussions would take place “throughout the next couple of days”, No 10 said, adding that the Foreign Office would lead talks over the form of an apology.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is already at the summit. One Foreign Office official said other Commonwealth countries “are responding positively to our offer of a structured dialogue” on an apology.

“The conversations at Chogm have been focused on the positive work this alliance can do together on issues like climate and trade,” they said. “By not shying away from difficult discussions about our past, we are building trust with our allies to focus on the big issues of the future.”
No 10 denied that Burnham’s comments had potentially embarrassed King Charles, who is already in Antigua and Barbuda for a pre-Chogm visit.

Buckingham Palace “was made aware in a timely manner”, Burnham’s spokesperson said. “The prime minister believes that being true to British values of decency and honesty means not shying away from these conversations.”

articles.title: How the EU can resist the divisive influence of the far right
articles.summary: Letters: Thomas Laffitte on the threats facing the European Union and Giorgio Re on why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-right
body: Your editorial rightly highlights the European far right’s maturing plans for Brussels’ political machinery (The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump, 27 October). Alongside these developments, the evolution of Euroscepticism itself deserves closer attention.

As I argued in a recent report from the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics, anti-EU politics may have entered a phase of “post-Euroscepticism”. The discourse remains, but the ambition to dismantle the union has increasingly given way to blocking the march towards an ever closer union while retaining the existing structure and exploiting it.

Ten years after Brexit, this shift reflects a deeper change in the global geopolitical order. With the return of great-power politics and the rise of geoeconomic rivalries, even radical nationalists may be reluctant to part with the great instrument of power that the EU has become. Giorgia Meloni’s unexpectedly pragmatic approach to EU cooperation is a prime example.

The EU’s institutional architecture offers some resilience. Its weak centre and dispersion of authority make it comparatively difficult for any one government to capture the entire polity. Yet this strength is also a weakness. Institutional divisions can translate into misalignment, dysfunction and, ultimately, decay. The EU will endure, but escalating nationalist rivalries risk compounding this tendency for inertia and the irrelevance that results.

This makes the negotiations over the next multi-annual financial framework (2028–34) particularly important. The EU must strengthen its competitiveness and strategic autonomy, while preserving the cohesion funds that remain one of its greatest success stories. Peripheral regions, where Euroscepticism has gained considerable ground, must not be forgotten.

The danger facing Europe is no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement. It also lies in the erosion of its capacity to act at a time when the return of geopolitics makes collective European power increasingly necessary. Thomas LaffitteResearch fellow, Brussels Institute for Geopolitics

• I felt compelled to write this letter after reading your editorial. I believe my feelings are shared by millions of Europeans whose voices are too often overlooked in today’s political debate – Europeans who value the freedom to live, study, work, do business and access healthcare across borders. And who believe that our common future deserves greater ambition.

As an Italian, coming from one of the six founding countries of European integration, and as a committed liberal conservative, I see no contradiction between defending individual freedoms, free enterprise, national identities and a stronger EU. Quite the opposite: in a world increasingly shaped by competing superpowers, European sovereignty can only be meaningfully exercised together.

However, defending Europe also requires acknowledging its shortcomings. Excessive bureaucracy, fragmented decision-making, sluggish economic growth and inadequate coordination on immigration and defence have contributed to public frustration. These deserve serious political answers rather than being dismissed as expressions of Euroscepticism.

That’s why I also believe that the strongest defence against nationalism must come from Europe’s democratic right and centre-right. We need European institutions that concentrate on what we can achieve better together: defence, external borders, strategic infrastructure, research and foreign policy. Mainstream conservative parties must resist the temptation to imitate nationalist rhetoric. They should instead articulate a confident, patriotic and genuinely pro-European alternative.

Some of Europe’s founding fathers, including Alcide De Gasperi, Konrad Adenauer and Robert Schuman, came from the Christian democratic tradition of the political centre-right. Their successors have a responsibility to carry that ambition forward.

I remain optimistic. Millions of centre-right Europeans believe in democracy, freedom and European unity. Their political voice could prove decisive in Europe’s future.Giorgio ReAgrigento, Sicily, Italy

articles.title: A diplomatic incident in Ealing over Kim Jong-un’s haircut
articles.summary: Brief letters: North Korean embassy | Reform UK newspaper | Wholemeal bread | Tarred and feathered | Lincolnshire’s actor-manager
body: Regarding your article on foreign embassies in residential London neighbourhoods (29 October), in 2014, a hairdresser in south Ealing put up a window poster with an image of Kim Jong-un and the strapline “Bad hair day?” They were offering a 15% discount on men’s haircuts. The next day, two besuited men from the nearby North Korean embassy turned up, demanding that the poster be removed. Both parties went to the police. No further action was taken.Toni Silver Eastbourne, East Sussex

• Thank you for warning me that the so-called “newspaper” produced by the so-called political party Reform UK may drop through my door (Report, 29 October). As my cat prefers to go outside in all weathers rather than use her litter tray, could you suggest other uses for this Farage farrago, or alternatively advise me how I can prevent it arriving at all?Anne CowperBishopston, Swansea

• One delicious, healthy and recognisably British bread, once widely available, is stoneground wholemeal. Since the rise of sourdough it has virtually disappeared (Admit it: the English love affair with European food has grown stale – we need a native cuisine we can be proud of, 27 October). A great investment in British culinary craft would be more wholemeal. Bring it back, please.Rev Nicholas BradburyOxford
• Are they still Tarring Neville in East Sussex (Letters, 28 October)? What did poor Neville do to deserve it? And is he feathered too?Sylvia McCormickBrighton, East Sussex
• Surely no one who ever travelled on the A1 through Lincolnshire could forget Boothby Pagnell, the great Victorian actor-manager?Martin StallionBraintree, Essex

articles.title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
articles.summary: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
body: Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”
He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.
Related: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?

“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.
Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.

In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.

At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.

Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.
“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.

Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.
“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.

The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

articles.title: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
articles.summary: Residents in Kyiv also warned of chemical attack and street-to-street fighting in false message sent by unknown party
body: Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.

The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.

Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”

A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.

In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”.

It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.

One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.

The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.

Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.

There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.

Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.

Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
Related: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries

According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.

The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region.

He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left.

Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said.

Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same.

Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

articles.title: ‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past
articles.summary: From 1945 to 1989 security police relied on tens of thousands of spies to suppress dissent. To rebuild trust, their files will finally be made public
body: Hungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust.

From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages.

For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks.
During his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections, Péter Magyar promised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power.

In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.
“A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook.

Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say.
“We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives.
Related: Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956

“As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today.

For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018.

Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now.
“People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?”

Placed side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material.

Many of the records will be incomplete, as the agent’s motivation, or extent of reporting, will remain unknown. Of the 60,000 people mentioned in the files, the archives include detailed files, background checks and statements for only 9,000 people. These will be released in February, after personal information, including details of health, addictions and sexuality, as well as information about victims, has been redacted in accordance with privacy laws.

Alexander Faludy, a freelance journalist and Anglican priest, read the files on his family almost two decades ago. His grandfather, György Faludy, spent more than three years in a Hungarian labour camp on fabricated accusations, and later while in exile wrote his book, My Happy Days in Hell.

One report in the files, by a Hungarian woman living in London who befriended Faludy’s grandmother as she was dying of cancer, made him particularly angry. “But then, I looked at the details of the informant. There was a really ominous part in her file, with names of relatives living in Hungary, including details of her elderly parents. Suddenly, my anger evaporated. I just felt very sorry for her,” Faludy said.

“Exile was very painful for my family, but it also conferred certain moral luxuries. And that makes me hesitant in terms of passing judgment on people for what they did if they had to stay in Hungary,” he added.

The identities of secret-service agents have long fascinated Hungarians. Since the 2000s, several partial lists have emerged, naming politicians and prominent artists. Many of them denied involvement, but the allegations alone were enough to plunge governments into political crises.
To date, not many former agents have spoken publicly about their experiences, and the subject remains taboo.

In July, Szemlélek, an independent, religious online journal, published a call for former agents to come forward. Religious figures were a known target of the state services and they were often blackmailed into reporting on their congregation. According to some estimates, 7-10% of them cooperated with the state.

So far, no one has volunteered to tell their story. “I think many people feel that there isn’t really much to speak about,” the paper’s editor-in-chief, Szilárd Szőnyi, told the Guardian. “Or they think that their story is so complex that they cannot, do not want to, or are not ready to tell it.”

Domokos Szokolay, a historian, said he was hopeful that this time “the release won’t turn into a public shaming, but that people will understand that these are complex issues”. His father, Zoltán Szokolay, a poet and politician, was outed as an informant in an unofficial list published in 2005.

Szokolay has yet to read all the reports on his father, who died in 2020. By speaking openly about transgenerational trauma, he hopes to reassure others who discover their loved ones were agents that they are not alone, and to encourage them to start conversations about what they find.

“There are so many family secrets or traumas that we can already talk about: if someone’s parent is an alcoholic, or a gambling addict. But people worry that they will be judged based on the agent files,” he said. “I know confronting one’s family history can be scary or even painful. But learning about it is always better.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: King Charles’s tour of the Caribbean has exposed the limits of the UK’s response to its past crimes
body: Good morning. Tomorrow, King Charles will formally open the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in St John’s, Antigua with a speech that addresses Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade with “unflinching honesty and sincere sorrow”.

It marks the culmination of a pivotal tour of the Caribbean that some observers warned could accelerate moves to remove him as head of state in several countries unless he does more to directly confront the monarchy’s historic links to enslavement.

Over the weekend, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, raised the stakes even higher when he published an article in the Guardian that signalled a historic shift. He went further than any previous prime minister towards offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, while ruling out financial reparations.

As leaders arrive for a meeting that reparations campaigners describe as the biggest crossroads for the Commonwealth since its creation, I spoke to our Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan, about apology, financial repair and the mounting pressure for a global reckoning.

UK news | Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.

Europe | Clashes erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities on Saturday after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched across France in a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services.

Cryptocurrency | Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replaced 90% of the ⁠amount stolen after a record $6.3bn hack of its platform by a group the FBI identified as being backed by North Korea.
Immigration | The Home Office is still putting asylum seekers on to planes to France weeks after the controversial scheme to remove them ended, the Guardian has learned.

US politics | A US judge dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice on Saturday, according to a court filing, bringing an end to his legal challenge over the newspaper’s reporting on his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein.

King Charles arrived in Antigua for the Commonwealth meeting on Friday after visiting the Bahamas, where he remains head of state, and Guyana, which replaced the British monarch with a president in 1970 after it gained independence from the UK four years earlier.

Although Charles has gone further than any of his predecessors in acknowledging his family’s historic links to slavery, the palace made it clear ahead of the visit that he wouldn’t be offering any formal apology – the king is constitutionally bound by the government’s stated position and can’t go further than it.
But the global context is inescapable at the end of a year that has seen “unprecedented developments” in the reparations movement, Natricia tells me.

In March a UN resolution, tabled by Ghana, declared the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity and called for reparatory justice, while Jamaica’s unprecedented slavery reparations petition to the king is due to be heard by the privy council next spring.
Amid this growing global pressure, campaigners told the Guardian ahead of the trip that if the king failed to meet this moment, it would raise serious questions about the future of the Commonwealth.

Then, in a move that took many by surprise, Andy Burnham opened the door to an official apology on behalf of the British state – while rejecting demands from Caribbean countries and campaigners for the UK to pay financial reparations, arguing that British people today could not be held liable for past wrongdoing.

This was a fairly seismic move – successive UK governments have refused both formal apology and reparations. In the UK, the rightwing media reacted with a focus on the impact on Charles himself, suggesting the king was “blind-sided” by Burnham’s announcement – although the palace insisted it had been made aware of it “in a timely manner”. In the Caribbean, Jamaica’s Sunday Observer went with the front page headline “Kicking and screaming!” to characterise the manner in which Britain had yielded to mounting international pressure.
Britain – and the Guardian’s – role in the slave trade

Nearly two centuries after emancipation, the true scale of Britain’s trafficking operations – which violently transported more than three million enslaved African men, women and children to colonial plantations in the Americas and Caribbean – is still not fully understood.

Last month, the Guardian revealed the findings of the Register of British Slave Traders, a three-year project by a team of specialist historians that documented for the first time the range of investors, from respectable men and women in provincial towns to kings and queens. It laid bare the extent of British involvement and underlined how slavery was not merely a footnote in British history, but helped shape the country.

Our extensive reporting forms part of the Cotton Capital series, which began in 2023 after the Guardian apologised for our own founders’ role in transatlantic enslavement, and launched a 10-year programme of restorative justice.
How has King Charles been received so far?

Ahead of the king’s tour, Labour MP, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who chairs the all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan reparations, argued that the royal family and UK government had failed to grasp the momentum behind the reparations movement. “I think it would be wrong to think that we can continue with platitudes,” she told the Guardian.
But after the king’s first speech last week in the Bahamas, where he referenced the country’s culture being “born out of darkness”, that’s precisely what many felt he was doing.

“There was a lot of disappointment,” says Natricia. She reported on a previous Chogm in Rwanda in 2022, when the then Prince Charles described “the depths of my personal sorrow” at the suffering caused by the slave trade. “I remember how strong and resolved he appeared to be four years ago, and it felt that had become much weaker,” Natricia says.

His reception across the Caribbean has been mixed, she tells me. In the Bahamas, he was greeted by a cheering crowd, despite a handful of protesters chanting “pay us what you owe”. “That respect and that love is still there,” says Natricia.

But when he arrived in Guyana, where he has no meaningful constitutional role, younger people interviewed by the Guardian were perplexed by his visit. “They told us: ‘His visit doesn’t have anything to do with me, so I don’t really care,’” Natricia says. And the prime minister of Antigua, Gaston Browne, who is hosting King Charles and Queen Camilla this week, stepped out of a Sunday morning church service alongside the royal couple to tell ITV News he would like his island nation to become a republic.

The palace was no doubt keen to avoid the misjudgements of the Prince and Princess of Wales’ tour to the region four years ago, when images of William and Kate shaking hands with Jamaican children through a wire fence were described as a throwback to colonialism, and the visit was overshadowed by calls for reparations and enduring anger at the Windrush scandal.

And yet little seems to have been done to address local concerns about the amount of money governments are required to spend hosting a monarch who, as Natricia says, “is not even willing to formally apologise for the way that his family has been enriched by centuries of enslavement and colonialism”.
How has Burnham’s intervention changed the mood?

Burnham has flown out to Antigua, where the shift in the UK government’s stance is being greeted with some caution. “People recognise that something quite remarkable has happened,” says Natricia, “but they’re saying this is not going far enough.”

Caribbean governments and campaigners have welcomed Burnham’s announcement, but remain clear that agreeing on forms of reparations is still a priority for the region. Their manifesto for reparations from the UK and other former colonial powers published in June includes a specific call for acknowledgement that women bore the brunt of enslavement as well as detail about compensation.
(If you want to learn more about why reparations is about much more than hard cash, read historian Olivette Otele’s piece for Cotton Capital here.)

Much now depends on how the conversations develop this week. Chancellor John Healey, foreign secretary Ed Miliband and former prime minister Gordon Brown will join Burnham at the summit to launch a new drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries. The UK will also offer support with the transition to renewable energy and getting smaller countries “a louder voice on the world stage”.
What next for the reparations movement this week and beyond?
Although not on the official Chogm agenda, calls for apology and reparation will be impossible to ignore in Antigua this week.

For campaigners, this gathering is the culmination of more than a decade of calls from Caribbean leaders for Britain to acknowledge its role. Natricia has spoken to organisers ahead of the meeting who are preparing to deliver their message on billboards and T-shirts, and at events including a beach vigil to remember the enslaved and the launch of a “global reparations caravan” – described by organisers as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture.
She contrasts this festival of activism with the royal visits she remembers growing up in the eighties, “when you might have a small protest, mainly by Rastafarians or Pan Africanists”.

“Something has happened in the Caribbean,” she tells me. “You see it in this insistence that we are going to just get rid of all the vestiges of colonialism, more countries removing the king as head of state, people becoming aware of their African heritage and being proud of that. I have seen this amazing shift.”

Natricia is personally astonished by the sea change in global momentum for formal apology and financial repair, even in the course of this year. For her, it means reparations remain firmly on the table – regardless of the UK government’s current stance.

“It’s a wave that has resulted in Andy Burnham doing what no other prime minister has ever done,” she says. “So to me, if they could go from ‘We will never apologise’ to discussing apology, we’re moving in the right direction, and now there is hope that this is not just a pipe dream, it’s something that could happen.”

“Britain is ready to spend £450m on EU students if it can join trade pact”, is the Guardian’s splash today, while the Express’s take is “‘We must not indulge the PM’s EU fantasy’”.

Tokyo’s annual Jimi Halloween turns the usual spooky season spectacle on its head, with participants dressing up as the mundane and the oddly specific – from a shop assistant spritzing customers with deodoriser to the elusive concept of “work-life balance”. articles.title: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds
articles.summary: Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election
body: The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.

There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.

A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.
Related: Israel election: what we know so far

The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.

The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.

Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.

Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.

But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.

A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.

The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”

The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.

A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.

There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

articles.title: Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition
articles.summary: Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
body: The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.
Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.

Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.

Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.

“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”

He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.

Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
Related: ‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli election

Eisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.

“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.

“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.
“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”

Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.

Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.

Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.

“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.
To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.

“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”

The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister has already made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.
One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in the resumption of war on Iran as a pretext for putting off political transition.
“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”
