• This article was amended on 2 November 2026. An earlier version said that one of Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot’s conditions for a potential coalition partnership with Arab parties was to “accept conscription”. In fact, the condition is to accept compulsory national service, which could be civil or military.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv says air raid warning app likely hacked after users receive false alerts
articles.summary: The app for a ⁠short time showed some areas ‌subject to false nuclear ‌and chemical alerts; temporary local ceasefire expires in southern Kherson. What we know on day 1,713
body: Ukraine’s air force said it suspected the country’s aid raid alert app – which is used across the country to warn people of the threat of airstrikes – had been hacked. On Sunday the app for a ⁠short time showed Kyiv and ​other areas ‌subject to nuclear ‌and chemical alerts. An erroneous message also said Russia’s hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to ‌have been subjected to enemy influence,” the air force said ​on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!”

Some hours later, Russia claimed a “massive cyber-attack” had hit its application designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats. “Attention! The mobile application of the Ministry of Emergencies of Russia has been subjected to a massive cyber-attack, enabling attackers to send false information to the public,” Moscow’s emergencies ministry posted on Telegram early on Monday.

Ukraine’s military said it evacuated 167 people from areas of southern Kherson region on Sunday as a temporary local ceasefire expired – two days after buses ⁠carried residents out of the ⁠Russian-held town of Oleshky. A six-day ​local ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding area was reached after mediation efforts by US first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo. Neither side reported violations after the truce began, in what one Ukrainian lawmaker described as the “biggest de-escalation since 2022”. US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume this month, having been effectively frozen since the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin warned local people to be particularly vigilant when the ceasefire ended and to “respond immediately to warnings about Russian attacks”. A Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity to AFP, expressed concern that the fighting would be “worse than before” when it resumed. Russian forces on the other side of the Dnipro river, had taken advantage of the calm of the past few days to amass new troops, transport ammunition stocks, and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions using surveillance drones, the officer said.

Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, Luke Harding reports from Kyiv. Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy company Rosneft. Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.

Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries – a key demand of Trump – if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles. Speaking to Fox News on Sunday, Zelenskyy said: “We said that if you want us not to attack Russia’s refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid.” Zelenskyy said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period. The Trump administration on Friday green-lit the sale of 500 Patriots to Ukraine, the state department said, but the Ukrainian president warned deliveries could take years. Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the interceptor missiles were dwindling.

articles.title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
articles.summary: British prime minister has now agreed to structured dialogue on reparatory justice but issue remains off formal Chogm agenda
body: British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.

Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.

“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.

“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”

Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.

“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.

He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”

Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.
He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”

An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.
“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”
Related: ‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the Caribbean

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.

Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.

“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”

Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.
Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.

The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.

As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.
Related: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit
King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.

On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

On Sunday Kemi Badenoch told broadcasters that an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.

“I would really like to sit down with my dear sister Kemi and explain to her so that she could get an understanding of what we are talking about,” Gonsalves said, adding that he would like to discuss how reparatory justice could help heal some of the fractures arising from Britain’s multicultural and ethnic tensions.

articles.title: Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash
articles.summary: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
body: An “inspiring” Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.

Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.

The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.

In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”
It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.

Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.
“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her.

“Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”
The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain, paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.

The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.
Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation.

articles.title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
body: Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.

Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.

The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”

Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.

In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.

Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.

Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.

Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.

Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”

Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title: The Guardian view on listening to people with learning disabilities: a matter of life and death
articles.summary: Editorial: The Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbed
body: The fear that so many felt as the death toll rose during the Covid pandemic was magnified for Fiona Walker. “I know from experience they wouldn’t have valued my life,” she says, in a new report on the treatment of people with learning disabilities during the crisis.

The 1.5 million people in the UK with learning disabilities, and their families, had reason for concern. Death rates in England were four to six times higher than average for people with learning disabilities. As is now well established, the pandemic did not create inequalities; it exposed and intensified them. People with learning disabilities die on average 19.5 years earlier than people without, and deaths are almost twice as likely to be classed as avoidable.

Learning the lessons means listening to people with learning disabilities and their family carers. Ms Walker and others were commissioners for the new How We Survive and Thrive report led by Learning Disability England, working with researchers from the University of Birmingham and Manchester Metropolitan University. It describes how families were abandoned by planners in the pandemic, though carers and communities gave welcome support. While care homes were failed, the needs of those living in family homes or community settings were often simply overlooked.

Recommendations include prioritising patients with learning disabilities and finding ways to increase rather than decrease support in a future crisis. But other improvements would help now as well as in the next public health emergency: ensuring people are included on the GP learning disability register, and providing accessible information and reasonable adjustments. Reactions to treatment can be wrongly taken as a refusal of care, when they really point to the need for easier to understand information, or the presence of a carer who can explain to or advocate for the patient. As Mencap has pointed out, such adjustments can be the difference between life and death.

While many carers and health workers may provide remarkable support and treatment, professionals are not immune from society’s prejudices. The shocking imposition of “do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation” decisions on people with learning disabilities in the pandemic may have partially reflected initial advice from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice). It said that patients should be assessed as scoring high for “frailty” – potentially affecting whether they received critical care – if they needed support with personal care, whatever the reason. Nice had to withdraw it. Testimony from patients with learning disabilities and their families suggests dangerous assumptions about patients’ quality of life also played a role. Those will be overcome only through sustained training and accountability.

Alarmingly, however, families and campaigners fear that progress made in recent decades is now being undone. Alongside cuts to social care packages and local support come profound challenges in healthcare. Important initiatives such as the Learning from Lives and Deaths scheme, examining the care received by people with learning disabilities and autism before their deaths, and mandatory training for healthcare staff on treating such patients, face growing funding pressures. The number of learning-disability nurses has fallen by a third since 2009 and student numbers are collapsing. That must be reversed. Learning disabilities should not mean a shorter life.

articles.title: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
articles.summary: Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
body: Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.

Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.
Related: Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy

Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.

Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.

“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.

Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sq km (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sq km (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”

The latest attacks came before a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.

“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.

Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.

Later on Sunday Ukraine’s air force and anti-disinformation centre said they suspected the country’s air raid alert system had been hacked, after false alerts of a radiation threat appeared on the application. The announcement came minutes after the end of the truce.
A separate app, which deals specifically with the Ukrainian capital, is still working normally, the Kyiv city authorities said.
Hours later, Russia’s emergencies ministry claimed that a “massive cyber-attack” had hit its own application designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.
There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged.

He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.

articles.title: Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police
articles.summary: Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
body: French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living have shaken a number of countries this autumn.

Violence erupted in the French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.
As the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.

In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.

The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged in one of the worst nights of urban unrest in France’s recent history.
In Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.

“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”

Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.
More than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.
Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.

More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.

Most of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.

Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.

In Portugal, riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.
The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.

In Albania, masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.

Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.

In Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”

In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones, Swiss media reported. A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.

In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.

articles.title: Tens of thousands protest against Narendra Modi regime in Delhi
articles.summary: Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
body: Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.

Led by the Congress party, India’s opposition alliance has brought together supporters from across the country, amid growing anger over a large-scale revision of the country’s voter roll that has seen 130 million names erased.

Opposition leaders have alleged the process gives Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) an electoral advantage, and have called for the resignation and impeachment of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. The BJP has denied the claims.

Addressing tens of thousands of party workers and supporters, the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said Kumar had “carried out the biggest crime. He has tried to silence the voice of people, strangulate our country.”

Gandhi said the opposition, united under the acronym India (Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance), would not let “democracy be finished in the country” and warned Modi: “You can’t run anywhere.”

The protest was one of the largest shows of opposition strength in years, taking place amid a wider resurgence of anti-government dissent which has been systematically crushed over the 12 years of the Modi regime.

The biggest challenge to the regime has come from youth-led protests that erupted over the summer – led by a movement that began satirically calling itself the “Cockroaches” – and forced the resignation of one of Modi’s cabinet ministers. Cockroach-led protests hit the streets again last month, also in opposition to the revision of the electoral rolls known as special intensive revision (SIR).

The opposition, in particular the Congress party, has become emboldened in the wake of the youth mobilisation. However, a significant trust deficit remains between the establishment opposition parties and the Cockroach movement. On Sunday, while Cockroach leaders had extended their support to the opposition rally, they did not attend themselves.
Congress leaders had publicly predicted that a million people would attend the rally, but in the end the numbers were in the tens of thousands and empty seats were visible in the protest arena.
The somewhat lacklustre turnout demonstrated the challenge still faced by Congress and its opposition allies in being seen as a formidable and viable challenger to the Modi government.

The opposition, led by Gandhi, has lost the last three general elections to the BJP as the parties have widely failed to counter the BJP’s muscular Hindu nationalist rhetoric. The Modi government has systematically gone after political opponents, leaving little space for dissent.

The majority of those gathered at the protest site on Sunday were party workers and organisers who had been bussed in, and there was very little evidence of a mobilisation of the young people who have been participating in the Cockroach-led protests. According to the opposition, many of their buses were stopped from entering Delhi by police barricades.

Shalini, a restaurant owner from Goa, said she was there “not for the opposition but because I am against the BJP and how they are trying to remove any avenue of dissent in this country. I’m not particularly for any opposition party.”

She said many questions still remained about the viability and support of that opposition, but she sensed a “groundswell of dissatisfaction with the BJP and the opposition is cashing in on it – good for them”.
Related: ‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streets

The issue of the revision of the electoral rolls first emerged last year, but recently erupted into a national scandal after an investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed irregularities and discord within the election commission over its implementation.

Millions of allegedly eligible voters have discovered their names have been left off the electoral rolls, with Muslims and minorities disproportionately targeted. This week, Human Rights Watch said the accusations raised “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections”.

Arwind Chaudhery, 48, said he too was not aligned with any party. “I am here because SIR has undermined our democracy and the situation has got so bad, it is beyond repair or rectification,” he said. “So it is natural that people will be driven out to protest and that is a ray of hope.”

The BJP have sought to dismiss the opposition protests as anarchy. The party’s president, JP Nadda, said Sunday’s rally would be the “nail in the coffin” for the opposition alliance. He said the protest was “not ​an act of respect for democracy. ‌It is a calculated conspiracy ​to plunge the nation into anarchy, ​all in the name of democracy.”

articles.title: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
articles.summary: Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes
body: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.

In a prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.
Related: Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended
Paralysed for more than a decade, the court sat at the core of rule of law clashes between the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.

Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk has sought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has been frustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.

The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.
Defending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.
He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.

Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians in Poland who seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”

He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev had joined the opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.

He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”
He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.
On Saturday, the European Commission urged Nawrocki to approve the new judges who were nominated by parliament, so the court could function in line with the constitution and EU law.
A spokesperson for the commission said its executive was “following closely” the events in Poland.

“It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the constitutional tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the court of justice of the European Union,” the spokesperson said, appearing to ally the bloc with the Polish government.

However, the spokesperson also highlighted that the European court of human rights issued an interim finding in May that obliged Polish authorities to “refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties” by judges who are still waiting to be sworn in.
The confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.
However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.
Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturday the legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.

The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded that the events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”

Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.

articles.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
articles.summary: A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
body: Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.

The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.

But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.

The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
Related: The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires

The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.

Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.

By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.

China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.

It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.

Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.

China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.

One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.

China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.

This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?

The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

articles.title: Britain should not issue apology over slave trade, says Kemi Badenoch
articles.summary: Tory leader says apology would be ‘navel-gazing distraction’ and would be used as lever for financial compensation
body: Kemi Badenoch has said an apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade would be a “navel-gazing distraction”, describing slavery as an evil “in which people from every continent and region participated”.
Speaking to broadcasters on Sunday, Badenoch also questioned whether it was worth future leaders attending the Commonwealth summit, given that it was now dominated by calls for reparations.

The Conservative leader made the comments as Andy Burnham said he was considering a formal apology, before he flies to the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next week.

In an article for the Guardian, Burnham said there would not be reparations in the form of financial compensation, but said he was prepared to engage in helping poorer countries restructure debt on more favourable terms.

Badenoch said leaders should be “honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today, especially given Britain’s leading role in ending the transatlantic slave trade”.

“If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?” she wrote in a social media post.
Badenoch said Burnham’s apology was unnecessary because of comments made by Tony Blair two decades ago. “The Commonwealth should be looking forward, not endlessly backwards,” she posted.

Badenoch told Sky News she believed that even if an apology was offered, campaigners would see it as a step towards financial compensation. “What I’m worried about is that this Chogm summit is yet another opportunity for people to start asking Britain for money because of the slave trade. We need to start looking at how we can bring the Commonwealth together – start looking forwards, not backwards.

“I don’t think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don’t think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash.”

Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the chancellor, John Healey, said it would be unfair for the British people to be hit financially for reparations when they had “no role” in the slave trade. “The prime minister has said, look, we are open to a discussion about an apology. He feels that that’s the right thing, particularly ahead of the Commonwealth leaders’ conference,” he said.

“But he doesn’t believe that reparations are the right approach, and considering a formal apology doesn’t mean accepting that British people now should accept the financial liability for any part in things that happened hundreds of years ago, in which they had no role.”

articles.title: ‘We’re making it worse’: Jacinda Ardern’s warning for Australian politicians
articles.summary: In her Sydney Opera House talk, the former New Zealand PM advised politicians to ‘rebuild trust by building financial security’
body: Jacinda Ardern, who now calls Sydney home, has delivered a message to Australian politicians from the stage of the city’s Opera House.
The former New Zealand prime minister turned academic told the audience on Sunday that politicians were exacerbating the problem of polarisation within society and needed to be better.

“We have a responsibility not to engage in binary thinking, not to engage in the language of violence, [but] to rebuild trust by building financial security in a time of deep insecurity,” Ardern said during a forum with the author Anna Funder.
“There are things we could be doing but right now we’re making it worse, not better.”
Related: Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor

In the past few decades, people across the world felt an increasing sense of insecurity as globalisation took hold, and they began attacking institutions such as the World Trade Organization, Ardern said.
Politicians offered proposals such as Brexit in response to the insecurity – saying “here’s what you blame” – which then paved the way for the rise of leaders like Donald Trump, she said.

The 46-year-old moved to Australia earlier this year. She purchased a house on the northern beaches in September and last week revealed she would be lecturing and mentoring at the University of Sydney.
Sunday’s talk was advertised as bringing together “two of the world’s leading thinkers” to discuss “can we disagree without becoming divided?”

“It’s not just that you hold a different opinion, it’s that you hold it so deeply that you have this view you’ve got moral clarity that is not being held by the other person,” Ardern said of the growing polarisation in public discourse.
“Therefore, you couldn’t possibly engage with them anymore. It’s made it much more difficult to create the discourse that we need to problem solve.”
Ardern and Funder were speaking a fortnight after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
The former New Zealand PM did not mention the incident explicitly but stressed politicians and leaders needed to be aware of the tone they set.
Social media had made it more difficult for people to change their views, she told the audience.

“Your opinions are recorded and held in time, and when so much of a healthy democracy is your ability to have debate and shift your views based on new evidence of information … that environment makes it more difficult,” Ardern said.
When she entered politics in 2008, she was not only the youngest sitting MP in the New Zealand parliament, but also the first to enter with an existing social media account.
At the time, many politicians – including Ardern – were excited to use social media to communicate directly with voters.
“I was so naive not to think about the fact that that meant the manipulation of information,” she said.
Her view of the online world changed on 15 March 2019 – the day of the Christchurch mosque shootings.

“A domestic terror attack came to our shores by someone who was radicalised on YouTube and who broadcast that mania in order to incite violence amongst other white supremacists using Facebook,” she said on Sunday. “That’s when I fully understood the weaponisation.”
Mistrust has been building for years and was now playing out in voters’ sense of grievance and insularity, Ardern said, adding that politicians had not been able to address it.
“At every point where you see this spike in mistrust, you see this disruption in what people are feeling and experiencing, and a failure of a political response to it.
“We’ve not fixed the core of the problem; in fact, we’ve then weaponised it with blame and distrust of others. We have not just a crisis of trust; we have a crisis of leadership.”
Ardern suggested empathy was part of the solution.
“What empathy brings to politics is a thing that we’re missing now. It brings humility, it brings curiosity,” she said. “If we had more humility in politics – what a difference that would make.”

articles.title: ‘What’s our crime?’: A Palestinian family’s fight to get care for son injured by Hamas rocket
articles.summary: Kinaan Dadou, 10, has been left disabled since 7 October 2023 as his parents struggle to find funding for specialist treatment
body: It was 7.30am on 7 October 2023 when a Hamas rocket exploded next to 7-year-old Kinaan Dadou. The rocket was aimed at the Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank but missed its mark by a few hundred metres, landing in front of Kinaan’s family home instead.

A piece of shrapnel struck Kinaan in the head. He stood rigid, his hands frozen to his sides, and screamed “Baba!” before collapsing to the ground. An Israeli soldier who passed by promised to call an ambulance. No help ever came. Kinaan’s parents rushed him to the hospital themselves, but it was six hours before a doctor arrived due to the chaos of the day. All the while, Kinaan’s brain was haemorrhaging.
It was the last time that Kinaan’s parents heard his voice.

Now 10 years old, Kinaan lies in a small bed in a persistent vegetative state. His limbs, pale and thin from atrophy, are covered with Mickey Mouse blankets. On the wall above his bed, his parents have taped pictures of Kinaan before the injury. The lively boy climbing trees and beaming into the camera bears little resemblance to the one below, whose one open eye moves listlessly across the bedroom. He is fed through a tube and breathes through a tracheostomy.

“I look at him and I ask him what he wants, what does he need? But he can’t respond, so I begin to cry. I think he’s in pain,” says Alaa Hassan Yakoub Dadou, Kinaan’s 47-year-old father, looking down at his son.

Kinaan’s case is unusual: a Palestinian child wounded by a Hamas rocket on the same day that about 1,200 people were killed in a Hamas-led attack on Israel. Three years on, Kinaan’s parents are still seeking help to pay for his treatment, finding themselves stranded between the Palestinian Authority (PA), which is responsible for healthcare in their area, and the Israeli authorities, who control virtually all facets of their lives.

The Dadou family live in the small village of Um Rukbeh, west of Bethlehem, a part of the occupied West Bank classified as “Area C”, where the Palestinian population lives under Israeli military rule.

The Palestinian Authority, which administers healthcare for Palestinians in Area C, gave some medical support for Kinaan early on – he underwent multiple brain surgeries and had a part of his skull removed – but his parents say it has refused to cover further specialist care and has been inconsistent in providing medication. Under Palestinian law, people with disabilities have the right to have at least 75% of their rehabilitation costs covered, while children also have the right to “obtain the highest possible standard of free healthcare services”.
Officials in the Palestinian ministry of health did not respond to questions.

Meanwhile, Israel, as an occupying power, also has certain obligations under international law to provide medical services, though it’s unclear if that extends specifically to Kinaan’s case. It has told a lawyer representing the family that Kinaan was injured in an area outside its jurisdiction, something the family questioned due to Israel’s de facto control over their daily lives. Israeli authorities control construction permits in Area C, including for bomb shelters, and dictate much of the family’s movement, complicating their efforts to get access to healthcare. Three months ago, they received a warning Israeli authorities would soon demolish their home.

The family has appealed to the Israeli government on humanitarian grounds. If they were Israeli and living in one of the increasing number of illegal settlements surrounding their home, the family says they would have had access to a bomb shelter and medical treatment.

“We’ve knocked on every door. The Arabs and the Israelis, it’s the same response. The Palestinian side says: ‘This isn’t our area.’ What’s our crime? That we happen to live among settlements? Neither side takes responsibility for us,” Alaa says.
Cogat – the Israeli body that oversees the Palestinian territories – did not respond to questions about Kinaan’s case.

Without outside help, the family has been unable to pay for the medical treatment that may improve their son’s condition. A specialist in Turkey said that, with an intensive recovery programme and further surgery, Kinaan’s condition could improve. But the cost of the treatment – about $250,000 (£190,000) – is far beyond what the family can afford.

“I pay 4,000 shekels [£950] per month just for his medication. I borrow from here and there, but it’s too much,” says Alaa. He used to work as a labourer in Israel, but has been out of work since Israel stopped issuing work permits to most Palestinians in the West Bank after the 7 October attack, leaving the family without income.
To save money, Kinaan’s mother, Woroud Dadou, has begun to perform some of the routine medical procedures herself. She changes her son’s breathing tube, saving the family £225 each month.

“I try to keep the tube as clean as possible so it lasts longer, but sometimes if I use the same one too long he begins to cough,” says Woroud, who adds she learned by watching doctors perform the procedures in hospital.

Alaa was told about a former colleague of his in Israel whose child was injured on 7 October. The child was flown to Germany for treatment and has since improved. He is happy for his colleague, but cannot help but wish Kinaan had access to the same treatment.
“If this was an Israeli child, even a settler child, do you think they’d have left him like this? He’d have been taken to the best hospitals. They would have done everything for him,” Alaa says.
“That’s what Israel does for its injured. It takes care of them. But when it comes to us, as a humanitarian case, it’s as though they’re saying: ‘Just give him his medicine until he dies.’”

Memories of Kinaan are scattered around the house. A little blue notebook is filled with his childlike scrawl as he practised letters: “pepper, cabbage, knight”. His parents are proud of his handwriting and said he dreamed of becoming a pilot when he grew up.

Though Kinaan is the middle child, he was the loudest of the three brothers. “Always putting them in order, like a little sergeant,” his father says, smiling. He recalls how, whenever he would come home from work, Kinaan would be waiting at the door, bringing his two siblings along to greet him.
Now only his wife greets him, and the sounds of play have mostly disappeared.

Kinaan appears to wake up, his face seemingly forming a smile as his father speaks. He keeps opening his mouth and pausing, as if about to speak, but no words come out. The room is silent, save for the sucking sound every time Kinaan takes a breath.

“We are realistic – we know he probably will never be the same as he was. But at least we want to relieve his suffering and relieve our guilt,” his father says. “It’s another kind of pain for a mother and a father, not knowing what exactly is hurting your child. That’s an enormous burden for a parent.”

articles.title: Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat was torched in an arson attack. Should it be rebuilt?
articles.summary: With the far right resurgent in Germany, experts are divided as to whether the dictator’s former mountaintop retreat is better restored or left a ruin
body: One of the last structural relics of Adolf Hitler’s dictatorship was conceived to project indomitable power. Last month it was destroyed in a suspected arson attack. Will it, and should it, be rebuilt?

The historic Nazi mountaintop retreat known as the Eagle’s Nest is perched on an Alpine peak at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft), with stunning views over southern Germany and Austria. In German, its design is known as Überwältigungsarchitektur, intended to overwhelm and intimidate.

Now, despite the efforts of 200 firefighters battling through the night, only charred ruins remain of the former guest lodge, tourist magnet and remembrance site destroyed in the blaze which started on 23 October. It is closed indefinitely.

“Even if a British air force bomb had struck the building on 25 April 1945, as it did most of the other structures in what was then the ‘Führer’s no-go zone’ on the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s former tea house … could scarcely have been more severely damaged than it was by the fire,” Munich’s Süddeutsche newspaper said.

The fire has triggered a debate about whether, and how, to rebuild at the toxic site for the next generation of visitors, while mitigating the never-quite-banished risk of creating a shrine for neo-Nazis.

While the places associated with Hitler’s victims, including the former concentration camps, are preserved in perpetuity, the question of how to treat the perpetrators’ artefacts remains fraught, particularly given the resurgence of the far right in Germany and in Europe more broadly.

Local authorities believe the fire was deliberately started by a 33-year-old suspect with a history of mental illness. The site, which is owned by the German state of Bavaria, attracts more than 300,000 people each year but was closed to visitors that day. No one was injured.

Bavarian state culture minister Markus Blume has said a commission of experts in heritage conservation, construction and Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance would be enlisted to help determine the future of the Eagle’s Nest.
Given the building’s inextricable links to the Nazi regime and its crimes, Blume said, “any reconstruction must do justice to this historical responsibility”.
The marvel of Alpine engineering, which took 3,800 workers just over a year to build, is known more prosaically in German as the Kehlsteinhaus, for the mountain it rests on.
After a coach ride on serpentine roads through five tunnels, visitors rode a brass-plated lift, built into the rock, for 41 seconds to reach its portal.

“The prestige project and the road leading to it cost about 30 million Reichsmarks, equivalent to about 130 million British pounds today,” said Nazi-era historian Felix Bohr, author of Before the Downfall: Hitler’s Years in the Wolf’s Lair, which is being published in the UK in November.
“Hitler loved architecture that made other people look small. He insisted on being involved in the planning and construction of propaganda buildings.”
The lodge was completed in 1938, and mainly used to welcome and impress state guests, diplomats and select foreign journalists.
Just a short distance down the mountain at the Obersalzberg complex was Hitler’s own residence, the Berghof, where he spent about a quarter of his 12 years in office.
“Important decisions about prosecution and crime, about war and genocide were taken there,” said Sven Keller, director of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, an educational facility at the site.

“The surrounding mountain scenery was used as a backdrop for the construction of Hitler’s ‘Führer’ image. It offered spectacular, awe-inspiring views, and demonstrated technical prowess to subjugate even this rough natural environment.”
Inside, it had many of the trappings of Nazi bling, including Untersberg marble donated by Mussolini, Venetian mirrors and plump green leather armchairs recalling an English country manor house.

Hitler is known to have visited the Eagle’s Nest only 14 times until 1939 and then never again due to the second world war’s outbreak, when the tea house no longer matched the warrior-statesman image he wished to project, Bohr said. Close associates including his companion Eva Braun still used it regularly, however.

After the war, Obersalzberg became a recreation centre for occupying US troops, but the last vestiges of the Berghof were torn down and hundreds of trees were planted in its place – a fateful decision that has served as a cautionary tale.

“The Americans and the Bavarian state tried to prevent it from becoming a pilgrimage site for old Nazis and Hitler admirers. It didn’t work. If anything, a hidden site in the woods is even more interesting and mysterious,” Keller said. Nazi swastikas were often found carved into the tree bark.
He said a 180-degree pivot toward clearly marking the site and exposing its history, including how it fit into the Nazi power apparatus, proved the healthier approach.

“Public accessibility creates transparency whereas barriers or fences encourage rumours and legends,” Keller said. “Today, a popular public trail crosses the site, and mundane activities such as hiking keep it from becoming a sacred space (for neo-Nazis).”
Keller said transparency should be the watchword going forward.
“I cannot imagine that those responsible would opt for [a] simple reproduction of Nazi architecture, but it also can’t be left as a ruin – those tend to be even more fascinating,” he said.

“Instead, we should find ways to integrate the material remains and new information and education, showing the temporal layers, including the use as a tourist destination since the 1950s. The fire added a new layer to the history to Obersalzberg, and this should be visible too.”

New political realities in Germany and Austria, where the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) and Freedom Party lead the respective national polls, will have to be taken into account as well, he said.

Bohr said that troubling context led him to oppose any reconstruction of the Eagle’s Nest. “Hitler’s megalomania should remain a ruin. My suggestion would be to secure the remaining structure as far as possible and to use it to convey the history of the site,” he said.
“Particularly in view of the strength of the AfD and the rise of right-wing extremism in Germany, the focus should be on coming to terms with Nazi ideology, not on restoring its stage sets.”

articles.title: Piles of rubbish, power cuts and potholes: anger grows over Johannesburg’s run-down infrastructure
articles.summary: The problems run deep in South Africa’s largest city. Will voters punish the ANC in next week’s local elections?
body: One week before the local elections in South Africa, the pavements and roads of the Johannesburg township Alexandra were filled with piles of rubbish, rotting in the heat. At the Jukskei River, its banks choked with rubble and litter, foul-smelling brown water flowed out of a culvert.

“We’ve got way too many challenges,” said Semadi Manganye, the chief executive of Alexandra Water Warriors, an environmental NGO that organises clean-ups of the river and plants trees on its banks. “If it’s not electricity, it’s water. If it’s not water, it’s waste.”

Manganye acknowledged the challenges of providing public services in a city whose population grew by 10% to 4.8 million between the 2011 and 2022 censuses. “I have an understanding of why they’re failing,” he said. “But we’ve got to mitigate against this – we knew that it was going to happen.”

On 4 November, up to 29 million South African voters will go to the polls for local elections amid deep discontent with the water cuts, power outages and potholes that plague the country’s 257 municipalities. Their problems are so deep that even the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has admitted: “Too many of our municipalities are failing to meet the needs and expectations of the people they are meant to serve.”

In the last financial year (2024-25), only 39 local governments, 15% of the total, received a “clean” audit from the country’s auditor general. Two-thirds are “financially distressed”, according to a parliamentary budget office report.

Nowhere are the problems more pressing than in Johannesburg, South Africa’s largest city and commercial capital. The city has been ruled by a series of unstable coalitions, with 10 changes of mayor in the past decade. Authorities have admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog. It is estimated that a quarter of the water bought by the municipal water body Johannesburg Water is lost to leaks.
At a public meeting in Rabie Ridge, a township in the city’s north-east, about 400 people berated the incumbent mayor, Dada Morero, and executives from Johannesburg’s electricity utility, City Power.

One person said she had had no power for six months. Another said her mother had been forced to turn to loan sharks after receiving energy bills as high as 6,000 rand a month when her monthly pension was 2,000 rand.
“If there is any organisation that is dysfunctional it is this organisation … it is failing,” one man said, drawing huge cheers from the audience.

Even some affluent northern suburbs are going without piped water for weeks at a time. After a month-long outage about six months ago, people in parts of Melville and Westdene have been unable to predict when they will get water since September.

“The word I’d use is desperate, because literally there’s been almost no water at all,” said Kate Spiller, a semi-retired management consultant. “During the day, there’s dribs and drabs. And then sometimes in the middle of night, my husband’s been able to fill a couple of five-litre bottles and then it’s gone dry again.”

Spiller and her husband drive 10 minutes almost daily to a mosque that has a borehole to fill up about a dozen five-litre bottles, which they use to take bucket showers. “It’s incapacitating … you’re always planning, you’re always thinking: ‘We need to get water, we’d better make a plan,’” she said.

“Overall, Johannesburg is providing the necessary services to our communities,” Morero said in an interview after the Rabie Ridge meeting. “Isolated areas where they don’t have [services], we are focusing on right now.”

He acknowledged parts of the inner city were without power, due to a “collapsed” substation, but blamed “vandalism” and criminals. “From time to time, with the JPMD [Johannesburg Metropolitan police department] we try to push back, but there are also syndicates who are also organised and affecting our infrastructure,” he said.

However, experts have said many city politicians and officials are themselves corrupt. An October report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime said: “Governance failure in the CoJ [city of Johannesburg] has given birth to a criminal ecosystem.”

“People in charge of the supply chain system can easily get backhanders,” said Rashid Seedat, a former city official and the executive director of the Gauteng City-Region Observatory, a research organisation.
“Of course, corruption is the metro police officer taking a bribe of 200 rand [and] a 200m rand tender. It’s across the board and endemic in the entire system and acceptable.”

The Democratic Alliance, South Africa’s second-largest political party, has mounted an energetic campaign in Johannesburg, under the 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor Helen Zille, to try to unseat the African National Congress (ANC) and its coalition partners, the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the populist Patriotic Alliance.

Zille, who is white, has previously caused controversy, particularly among black voters, including for tweets in 2017 that said colonialism was not completely negative. However, viral stunts that have drawn attention to Johannesburg’s infrastructure issues, such as Zille snorkelling in an enormous flooded pothole, have helped to put the DA ahead of the ANC in the polls (voters choose parties and councillors, who in turn elect the mayor).

The DA has polled between 29% and 36% in October, compared with 22% to 27% for the ANC, which is fielding three possible mayoral candidates amid factional infighting. However, this may not be enough for Zille to form a coalition, analysts say.

“In order to understand Joburg, you actually have to zoom out a bit and look at all of Gauteng [province],” said Ziyanda Stuurman of Africa Practice, a consultancy. “Over the last decade, and especially since 2021, there’s been this very clear working relationship between the ANC, EFF and ActionSA across the three municipalities [Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni].
“Once in-principle coalition arrangements are agreed to, you’ve seen the EFF back ANC and ActionSA mayors across all three cities and there’s been a negotiation keeping in mind all three.”

Stuurman said a coalition similar to recent ones could lead to five more years of decline in Johannesburg. “It’s been much more horse-trading than it actually has been about the city’s best interests.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says Moscow must be shown that support for Kyiv will not diminish; US says interest also growing for limited Black Sea ceasefire. What we know on day 1,712
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Oleshky ceasefire shows that de-escalation steps with Russia are possible, while the US says there is growing interest for a truce in the Black Sea. Zelenskyy said the humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky “clearly demonstrates that de-escalation steps are possible when Russia is the one put in a position where it has to take steps toward de-escalation”. The Ukrainian president also said at a news conference with his Turkish counterpart, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in Istanbul on Saturday: “Strong decisions are needed to bring peace. At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish. This is all the more important given that a humanitarian operation took place in Oleshky, in the Kherson region, over the past few days.”

In the US, the secretary of state said there was growing interest in the international community in facilitating a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to ensure unfettered energy and grain shipments by Russia and Ukraine. Marco Rubio said the US was reviewing proposals by Turkey and India to get grain shipments moving, even ⁠as the US continued to press ⁠for a broader negotiated settlement of the war. There was growing interest – if not momentum – in partial deals such as halting attacks on ships carrying grain and, in some ​cases, energy in the Black Sea, Rubio said ⁠on Saturday. “This is threatening the world for food security and ‌some energy security as well,” he told reporters in Atlanta after a ‌two-day G20 foreign ministers’ meeting that involved Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov despite objections from European and Canadian leaders.

Zelenskyy said at the Istanbul news conference that he and Erdoğan had discussed the prospects of holding trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in early November, as well as other possibilities “including ways to involve Türkiye and all of Europe”. Erdoğan, meanwhile, said attacks aimed at civilian vessels in the Black Sea were unacceptable, urging Russia and Ukraine to “act responsibly”. “We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered.” Talks aimed at restoring the safety of navigation in the Black Sea would continue, Erdoğan added. Zelenskyy accused Russia of making the situation in the Black Sea difficult.

In Ukraine, evacuees from Oleshky were reunited with loved ones after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday amid the US-brokered localised ceasefire. Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Evacuees told Agence France-Presse that some residents had to eat grass and dogs to survive and that their rescue following a humanitarian truce was a “blessing”. “People were cooking grass. They’d grow it as there was nothing to eat,” said Valera, a 29-year-old former resident who did not give his last name. “Lots of people were blown up. There were piles of bodies on the roads, loads of cars. In short, it was brutal ... terrifying.” The truce in the southern Kherson region was expected to continue until Sunday evening.

Russia said on Sunday a drone had struck an “industrial enterprise” east of Moscow overnight, after Ukraine claimed it had hit a major oil refinery. Gleb Nikitin, governor of Nizhny Novgorod region, reported a “massive drone attack” during the night in which an “industrial enterprise in the Kstovo district sustained significant damage”. Preliminary information suggested there were no casualties, he added, without specifying the plant’s activities. Ukrainian media reported an attack on the Kstovo oil refinery, calling it “one of Russia’s largest oil refineries, producing fuel and lubricants”. On Saturday Ukraine’s ‌general staff said the military hit a major missile ⁠fuel ⁠producer in ​Russia’s Rostov region overnight, ⁠causing a fire and damaging four ⁠production facilities.
